title: Replace the conventional L1 instruction cache with an Execution Trace Cache
decision: Use the Execution Trace Cache as the primary L1 instruction cache, storing already-decoded uops in predicted-execution-path traces rather than ordinary IA-32 instruction bytes.
alternatives_or_rejected: A conventional instruction cache would require repeated IA-32 decoding and would incur additional branch-target delivery delay; the paper presents the Trace Cache as the alternative, but does not describe a formal design-selection process beyond these arguments.
rationale: IA-32 decoding is cumbersome and a high-bandwidth decoder would require several pipeline stages. Caching decoded uops removes decoding from the normal execution loop, reduces branch-misprediction recovery latency, and allows the decoder to operate at only one IA-32 instruction per clock.
outcome: The Trace Cache holds up to 12K uops, delivers up to three uops per clock, and is used for most instruction execution; decoding occurs primarily on Trace Cache misses.
quote_as_recalled: By caching the uops of the previously decoded instructions in the Trace Cache, the NetBurst microarchitecture bypasses the instruction decoder most of the time.
weakest_point: The paper strongly contrasts the Trace Cache with conventional instruction caches, but does not present that contrast as a detailed quantified design-study decision.

title: Deepen the pipeline aggressively to pursue much higher clock frequency
decision: Use a pipeline roughly twice as deep as P6, reducing the amount of logic performed per stage in order to pursue a substantially higher operating frequency.
alternatives_or_rejected: The P6-depth pipeline and the shallower pipelines of earlier Intel processors are the explicit comparison points; the paper does not describe a separate rejected NetBurst pipeline candidate.
rationale: Higher clock rates require less logic per cycle. The authors explicitly acknowledge the trade-off: deeper pipelines reduce efficiency at a given frequency and increase the cycle cost of events such as branch misprediction and cache misses, but the frequency gain was judged worthwhile for the design target.
outcome: The Pentium 4 uses a 20-stage misprediction pipeline versus 10 stages for P6 and was designed for a greater than 1.6× higher frequency target on the same process technology.
quote_as_recalled: There are tradeoffs when designing for higher clock rates.
weakest_point: The paper does not give a detailed optimization point showing why approximately 20 stages was quantitatively superior to every intermediate depth; it explains the design philosophy and comparison with P6.

title: Run the critical ALU execution loop at twice the main processor clock
where_in_paper: Integer and Floating-Point Execution Units / Low Latency Integer ALU, pp. 8–9
decision: Make the most common simple integer ALU operations execute at twice the main processor clock rate, using a very small high-speed ALU-bypass loop.
rationale: Approximately 60–70% of uops in typical integer programs use the key integer ALU loop. Running those operations at half the main-clock latency improves common-case program execution. The high-speed loop is deliberately kept small so its metal length and loading remain low; less-frequent functions are kept outside it.
outcome: The processor achieves an effective one-half-main-clock ALU latency for dependent operations, using staggered addition so only a 16-bit adder and its input muxes need to complete within a fast-clock interval.
quote_as_recalled: This high-speed ALU core is kept as small as possible to minimize the metal length and loading.
weakest_point: The paper describes the frequency and physical organization very clearly, but it does not frame the choice as an explicit comparison against a conventional single-speed ALU in a formal alternatives section.

title: Optimize common cases rather than making every execution unit equally fast
where_in_paper: Integer and Floating-Point Execution Units / Low Latency Integer ALU, p. 8
decision: Put only the frequent simple integer operations in the critical low-latency ALU loop and place less-frequent functions such as multiply, shifts, flag logic, and branch processing elsewhere.
rationale: The paper's stated design principle is to optimize overall performance by handling common cases as fast as possible. Keeping infrequent operations out of the critical loop makes the high-speed path physically smaller, reducing metal length and loading and allowing the frequency target to be achieved without making every function part of the fastest loop.
outcome: Two double-speed ALUs handle simple integer operations, while multiply, shifts/rotates, flag processing, and branches use other execution hardware.
quote_as_recalled: The execution units are designed to optimize overall performance by handling the most common cases as fast as possible.
weakest_point: The paper explicitly states the common-case principle and lists functions kept outside the loop, but does not explicitly say that a fully unified fast ALU was the alternative rejected.

title: Allow execution bandwidth to exceed front-end and retirement bandwidth for bursts
decision: Provide execution dispatch capacity of up to six uops per main clock even though the front end and retirement machinery sustain three uops per clock.
rationale: The excess execution bandwidth is intentional: it permits peak bursts above the normal three-uop rate and gives the schedulers greater flexibility in choosing among execution resources. The deeper out-of-order window lets ready instructions accumulate so execution resources can exploit available parallelism.
outcome: Two fast execution ports can dispatch up to two operations per main clock, while load and store ports each dispatch one; collectively they can dispatch up to six uops per clock against three-uop front-end/retirement bandwidth.
quote_as_recalled: This dispatch bandwidth exceeds the front-end and retirement bandwidth, of three uops per clock, to allow for peak bursts of greater than 3 uops per clock.
weakest_point: Calling the six-versus-three bandwidth relationship a 'design decision' is an interpretation; the paper states the architecture and its rationale but does not narrate a competing design being rejected.
